audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Saturday, October tenth, twenty twenty-six. Lighter news cycle this weekend, but a couple of stories land right in the middle of your practice, so let's take them slowly and dig in.

Let's start with the story I most want you to sit with, because it's local, concrete, and lands squarely on your public-institution AI governance thesis. Microsoft has published a case study on Thompson Rivers University — your nearest institution, right there in Kamloops — rolling out Microsoft 365 with AI tooling. The framing is interesting and a little revealing: it's pitched around speeding up security threat review and preparing the institution for generative AI. In other words, this isn't being sold as a flashy chatbot launch. It's being sold as infrastructure and risk management. That's the right instinct, and it's also exactly the entry point you've been building your governance lens around.

Here's why this matters for your work specifically. When a Canadian public university adopts enterprise AI through a platform like Microsoft 365, a whole set of questions gets triggered that most institutions handle badly or quietly. Where does the data live — is it resident in Canada, or routed through US data centres? How does FIPPA apply when faculty and staff start feeding student records, research, and internal documents into Copilot-style tools? Who owns the audit trail? What's the retention policy on prompts? A Microsoft case study will frame all of this as solved and seamless, because that's what case studies do. Your job — and your content opportunity — is to be the voice that says: here are the seven questions a BC public institution should answer before, not after, they flip the switch. You now have a named, local, credible anchor to hang that piece on. I'd genuinely consider writing it this week. TRU as the case study, the governance checklist as the payload. That's a thought-leadership post that positions you precisely where you want to be heading into twenty twenty-seven.

Staying in higher ed, University Affairs ran a thoughtful piece on faculty well-being in the age of generative AI. The core argument is that when every student has an AI assistant in their pocket, the writing instructor's job becomes simultaneously harder and more essential. It's an opinion piece, but it's a useful one, because it surfaces the human and labour dimension of AI adoption that enrollment and marketing conversations tend to skip over. If you're advising an institution on AI-enabled recruitment or student communications, it's worth remembering that the faculty experience shapes the brand too. Burned-out, suspicious faculty undermine the very student experience the marketing promises. The governance conversation and the well-being conversation are the same conversation, just viewed from different seats.

And then a sharp cautionary note from the frontier labs. Anthropic has quietly turned off live internet access for all of its internal AI evaluations, until further notice. The reason is blunt: they concede they can't reliably control their own AI agents. Think about that for a moment. The company building some of the most capable models in the world is walling its own testing environment off from the open internet because the agents behave unpredictably when they can reach out and act. Now hold that next to every vendor pitch your clients are receiving about autonomous agents that will book the meetings, answer the enquiries, and run the campaigns. The lesson isn't that agentic AI is useless — it's that the people closest to the technology are treating autonomy as a containment problem. When a brokerage or an enrollment office asks you whether they should deploy an autonomous agent, this is your evidence base for counselling a sandboxed, human-in-the-loop rollout rather than a full handoff. The frontier labs aren't trusting their own agents on the open web yet. Neither should your clients.

On the marketing front, a small story with an outsized signal for you. An agency called C-360 published its five marketing priorities for twenty twenty-seven, and sitting right up there alongside brand strategy is AI-driven search. I flag this not because the agency itself matters, but because of what it represents: generative search visibility is officially crossing over from the thing early adopters talk about to the thing agencies list in their annual planning decks. That's the adoption curve you've been positioning your AI Search Readiness product against. The timing is good for you. There's a window — call it the next twelve to eighteen months — where the concept is mainstream enough that clients understand the question, but the practice is immature enough that few agencies can actually audit how a brand appears in Google AI Mode, AI Overviews, ChatGPT, and Perplexity. That gap between awareness and capability is your market. The content angle writes itself: everyone's now naming AI-driven search as a priority, but naming it and auditing it are very different things — and here's what an actual audit looks like.

Two more from the CMO world worth a quick listen. Volkswagen's chief marketing officer, Rachael Zaluzec, talked through the brand's expanded partnership with U.S. Soccer and NBCUniversal, and the theme was building emotional connection through partnership rather than brute-force paid reach. And over at Free People, the CMO explained at Advertising Week why the retailer deliberately ceded creative control to the musician Willow in their collaboration — what he called cultural co-authorship. Both stories circle the same modern truth: control is no longer the asset it used to be. The brands winning cultural relevance are the ones comfortable sharing the pen. That's a useful frame when you're advising institutions and brokerages that instinctively want to lock down every message. Sometimes the credible move is to let the partner, the creator, or even the community shape the story.

Now to higher education, and the story you'll want on your radar for every BC conversation this quarter. The Globe and Mail reports that British Columbia's universities and colleges are in limbo, waiting on the release of an independent review of the sector. Until that review lands, institutions are operating in uncertainty about funding, governance, and operations — and uncertainty is corrosive to planning. Enrollment teams can't set strategy confidently, finance teams can't budget cleanly, and marketing teams get told to hold. For anyone working across BC higher ed, this is the backdrop to everything right now. Watch for the release date, and watch for what it says about international enrollment caps and funding models in particular, because that's where the operational consequences will bite hardest. When it drops, it'll reset a lot of conversations at once.

Two stories from south of the border round out the picture, and they both point the same direction — toward Canada's advantage. First, the US is probing nine universities over their use of J-1 visas, with allegations that institutions used the program to undercut American researchers' wages. Alongside it, a suspension affecting several major employers threatens to delay permanent-residency applications for foreign workers. Second, Washington is seeking an expedited appeal over the blocked four-year time limits on international students, keeping that policy on hold but very much alive. Put these together with everything we've tracked over the past week — the OPT fee proposals, the internship legal battles, the general climate of uncertainty — and the message to globally mobile students is consistent: the US is an unpredictable bet right now. That's the context in which Canada is actively courting more graduate international students. Every institution you work with in the Canadian market should be sharpening its message to exactly the students who are now hesitating about America. The opportunity is real, but it's a race, and the window won't stay open forever.

Closer to home, the twin campaigns in Kamloops continue to dominate local news, and the themes are consistent. On the municipal side, the mayoral candidates are staking out sharply different positions on public safety — a continuation of the campaign we've been following, where debt, taxes, and crime have defined the debate. And on the provincial side, candidates canvassing door to door say affordability is the single issue voters raise most. Those two threads — safety and affordability — are the emotional weather of the region right now, and they'll shape everything from consumer confidence to how families think about property. Worth keeping in the back of your mind for any real estate or local conversation.

There's also a difficult local crime story reaching its conclusion: the trial over a Kamloops mutilation case is heading to closing arguments, with the defence now arguing a revenge motive. It's a grim one, and I'll leave it there, but it's been a significant local story and it's nearing resolution.

On the global stage, the story with real consequences is an energy and geopolitics one. President Trump has announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which he reportedly agreed to after Ukraine ignored half a dozen US requests to stop striking Russian oil refineries. President Zelensky called it a gift to Putin and an investment in a war that should be ended, not prolonged. This has triggered a fresh crisis between Washington and Kyiv, and it threatens to derail the administration's own push for a settlement. Beyond the diplomacy, keep an eye on what any shift in Russian diesel flows does to global fuel prices — energy costs ripple into inflation, and inflation ripples into the Bank of Canada's thinking, which eventually ripples into mortgage rates and the real estate market your practice touches. It's a long chain, but it's a real one.

And a lighter footnote from the same orbit: Trump reacted furiously to losing the Nobel Peace Prize, which went instead to Navi Pillay, a former judge of a court his administration has sanctioned. Not consequential on its own, but another data point in the ongoing friction between the US administration and international institutions — the same friction that's reshaping where students, researchers, and talent choose to go.

Finally, a quick BC safety note. High winds on Friday knocked out power for more than twenty thousand households across the Lower Mainland and Sunshine Coast, and delayed B.C. Ferries sailings. Nothing catastrophic, but it's the first real reminder that fall storm season has arrived. If you've got family or travel plans on the coast in the coming weeks, it's worth building in a buffer for wind-related outages and ferry delays. With properties in Langley and Vancouver, it's also a prompt to make sure the usual storm-season basics are handled before the pattern intensifies.

That's your Saturday, Midya. If you do one thing with this briefing, make it the Thompson Rivers piece — a named local institution adopting enterprise AI is the perfect, timely anchor for the governance checklist content you've been meaning to write, and the market is clearly ready for it. Keep the BC post-secondary review on your watch list; when it lands it'll move a lot of conversations at once. And enjoy the long weekend — the news will keep, and the quiet is a good moment to get ahead of the writing rather than just reacting to it. Talk soon.
